name: Senovilla Universe With No Singularity
description: A universe filled with radiation and arranged around an axis, which contracts, is densest at one moment, and expands again, with no big bang and no singularity anywhere, found by José Senovilla in 1990. It satisfies the energy conditions and is globally hyperbolic, and the singularity theorems leave it alone because it has no closed trapped surface and its expansion falls to zero far from the axis.
convention: The constant $a$ is an inverse length. We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Does a universe full of ordinary matter have to begin at a singularity? Amal Kumar Raychaudhuri published the first argument that it does in 1955, for matter that falls freely and does not rotate [raychaudhuri1955, senovilla1998, senovilla2007]. The theorems Roger Penrose proved in 1965 and, with Stephen Hawking, in 1970 ask for gravity that attracts, a well behaved causal structure, and one thing more, such as a closed trapped surface [penrose1965, hawkingpenrose1970, chinea1992]. By 1990 it was widely believed that a universe filled with hot radiation "should be singular due to the powerful singularity theorems" [senovilla2007].¶José Senovilla's answer, published in May 1990, was a single exact solution with no singularity anywhere [senovilla1990]. Picture radiation, with a pressure one third of its energy density, piled up around an axis and thinning out in every direction away from it [senovilla1990, chinea1992]. Its energy density is $15a^2c^4/(8\pi G\cosh^4(act)\cosh^4(3a\rho))$, with $1/a$ a length that sets the scale, and the fluid contracts for $t < 0$, is densest at $t = 0$, and expands from then on [chinea1992]. "The most remarkable feature is the absence of an initial singularity", Senovilla wrote, with the curvature and the matter "regular and smooth everywhere" [senovilla1990]. Ten days later John Maddox wrote that the latest solution of Einstein's equations "has the particular interest of making the Big Bang less than a mathematical necessity" [maddox1990].¶Could a singularity be hiding where the coordinates do not reach? Two years later Francisco Javier Chinea, Leonardo Fernández-Jambrina, and Senovilla followed every light ray and every freely falling particle, and each one runs on for ever: it can be continued to arbitrary values of its affine parameter [chinea1992]. The collapse stops because the radiation pushes back: it is densest on the axis, and "the gradient of pressure does not allow for the formation of a singularity and causes a bounce from which the matter expands" [chinea1992]. Raychaudhuri's argument of 1955 assumed matter with no such push, so it does not apply [senovilla1998]. The bounce can happen at any density: the constant $a$ is free, and the greatest density, $15a^2c^4/8\pi G$, "can be chosen as large or small as we like" [chinea1992].¶The theorems of Penrose and Hawking let it slip past [chinea1992]. Their energy conditions hold, and the whole spacetime can be predicted from any one moment of $t$: it is globally hyperbolic, the strongest of the causality conditions [chinea1992, senovilla2007]. It lacks the one thing more: it has no closed trapped surface, no slice of space that closes on itself, and no point whose light cone converges again [chinea1992]. Everywhere in this universe light sent outward from the axis spreads and light sent inward converges [chinea1992]. The simplest of the theorems needs the expansion to stay above some positive number over a whole slice of constant time, and here the expansion is positive at every point after $t = 0$ and still falls toward zero far from the axis [chinea1992]. Chinea, Fernández-Jambrina, and Senovilla concluded that "the initial condition is essential for the development of singularities" [chinea1992].¶Senovilla's universe is one of a family [ruiz1992]. Eduardo Ruiz and Senovilla built the family that same year, by taking each metric component to be a function of time multiplied by a function of radius, and found big bangs, timelike singularities, and complete universes among its members [ruiz1992]. Trade $\cosh(act)$ for $\sinh(act)$ in Senovilla's metric, for one, and the big bang is back, a finite time in the past [chinea1992]. Among the family's fluids with pressure a fixed fraction of the density, the complete ones are the radiation fluids alone: a stiffer fluid has a singular density and a softer one a singular Weyl tensor [fernandezjambrina2002]. Until 1995 every complete universe known was cylindrically symmetric, with a metric diagonal and separable in coordinates at rest with the fluid [senovilla2007]. Fernández-Jambrina and Luis M. González-Romero found room for many more in 2002: complete universes filled with a stiff fluid, a family that depends on two free functions [fernandezjambrina2002].¶So is this our universe? Its discoverers said no, and Raychaudhuri, by then in his seventies, said why in 1998: in a universe with no rotation and no singularity, every scalar built from the matter averages to zero over the whole of spacetime [chinea1992, raychaudhuri1998, senovilla2007]. Alberto Saa and Senovilla each answered that the same averages vanish in the open Friedmann universes, big bang and all, and Senovilla proposed averaging over space at one moment [senovilla2007]. He proved that version in 2007: an open universe without rotation that expands everywhere, and whose matter has a nonzero average over space, has geodesics that end in its past, a singularity [senovilla2007]. His own universe escapes because its radiation thins out so fast away from the axis that the average density over all of space, at any moment, is zero [senovilla2007]. He wrote that "one could then say that the regular models are not cosmological" [senovilla2007].

related.text: The same cylindrical symmetry with nothing in it but gravitational waves. Both metrics are diagonal, with a plane of $t$ and $\rho$ that is conformally flat, so radial light rays run at 45° in both [fernandezjambrina2002].
Inhomogeneous cosmologies with the same two commuting symmetries of space, in vacuum and wrapped into a torus [ruiz1992].

The universes whose big bang Senovilla's does without. One class of metrics, with a function of time for a scale factor and four parameters, holds every Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker universe and Senovilla's as well [senovilla1996].

de Sitter's universe also contracts, bounces, and expands with no singularity. It has closed trapped spheres and escapes Penrose's theorem because its slices of constant time are compact, and it violates the strong energy condition, which Senovilla's universe keeps [senovilla1998].

A complete universe that satisfies the strong energy condition, as Senovilla's does. It has compact slices and points whose light cones converge again, and it escapes the theorems because the generic condition fails along its world lines at rest [senovilla1998].

Another universe that bounces with no singularity, this one of spinning dust in the Einstein-Cartan theory. It is homogeneous and it violates an energy condition of the singularity theorems, which Senovilla's universe keeps [hehl1974, trautman2006].
A universe whose bounce comes from loop quantum cosmology, at a critical density of about 0.41 of the Planck density [ashtekar2011status].

coordinates.name: Cylindrical

parameters.description: Inverse length that sets every scale; the energy density of the radiation is greatest on the axis at $t = 0$, where it is $15a^2c^4/8\pi G$, and so is the Kretschmann scalar, $792\,a^4$

coordinates.convention: We use Senovilla's cylindrical coordinates $(t, \rho, \phi, z)$, at rest with the fluid, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\rho$ and $z$ lengths. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
